2027-07-12.title: Monday of the Fifteenth Week in Ordinary Time
readings: A new king arose over Egypt, who did not know Joseph
Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth
2027-07-12.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 15 (Year I). From today the first reading is the Book of Exodus, read on the weekdays of weeks 15 and 16 and into week 17, the story of the oppression, the call of Moses and the liberation of Israel. The Gospel closes the mission discourse of St Matthew, chapter 10. Psalm verses are given in NRSV numbering. Liturgical colour: green.
2027-07-12.verse: Those who find their life will lose it, and those who lose their life for my sake will find it.
theo: With today's reading the Book of Exodus begins, and the story changes. A family has become a people, and a people has become a problem for a new regime. The book opens with names: the sons of Israel who came to Egypt with Jacob, seventy persons in all. In a few lines a whole era passes: “Then Joseph died, and all his brothers, and that whole generation. But the Israelites were fruitful and prolific; they multiplied and grew exceedingly strong, so that the land was filled with them.” God's blessing from the first pages of Genesis, “Be fruitful and multiply,” is being fulfilled in the foreign land. Then comes the sentence that turns the page: “Now a new king arose over Egypt, who did not know Joseph.” Joseph, who saved Egypt from famine, has been forgotten; gratitude is short-lived when power is at stake. The king speaks like a frightened man: “Look, the Israelite people are more numerous and more powerful than we. Come, let us deal shrewdly with them, or they will increase and, in the event of war, join our enemies and fight against us and escape from the land.” A minority has become a threat to national security, and the answer is to be “shrewd,” step by step. First forced labour: “they set taskmasters over them to oppress them with forced labor. They built supply cities, Pithom and Rameses, for Pharaoh.” Then harsher: “The Egyptians became ruthless in imposing tasks on the Israelites, and made their lives bitter with hard service in mortar and brick and in every kind of field labor.” The bitterness will be remembered every year at the Passover table. But the plan does not work. “The more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied and spread, so that the Egyptians came to dread the Israelites.” The blessing of God cannot be stopped by a decree. So the king turns to murder. The Hebrew midwives Shiphrah and Puah, whom the Lectionary passes over, “feared God” and let the boys live: the first act of conscientious refusal in the Bible, and Scripture records their names while the king's name is not given. Then Pharaoh orders all his people: “Every boy that is born to the Hebrews you shall throw into the Nile, but you shall let every girl live.” The river that gives Egypt its life becomes a place of death, and in tomorrow's reading a baby in a basket will be drawn out of it. Notice that it is one king and one policy, not a whole people: the next chapter shows an Egyptian princess saving the child. The Psalm is the song of those who came through such a time: “If it had not been the Lord who was on our side, when our enemies attacked us, then they would have swallowed us up alive.” “We have escaped like a bird from the snare of the fowlers; the snare is broken, and we have escaped. Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth.”

The Gospel brings the mission discourse to its end with some of the hardest words of Jesus. “Do not think that I have come to bring peace to the earth; I have not come to bring peace, but a sword.” In the same discourse he has told his disciples to bring peace into every house (Matthew 10:13), and he is the Prince of Peace. The sword is not a weapon of war. It is the knife that cuts, the line that falls between those who accept him and those who refuse him; the words that follow are taken from the prophet Micah, who described how families break up in a time of trial (Micah 7:6). Jesus is not telling anyone to quarrel with their parents; elsewhere he defends the duty to honour father and mother (Matthew 15:4–6). He is saying that no loyalty, however sacred, may stand above him: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me.” In many families, in every age, the decision to follow Christ has cost a person the peace of the home, and Jesus does not hide it. “And whoever does not take up the cross and follow me is not worthy of me.” It is the first mention of the cross in the Gospel of Matthew, before Jesus speaks of his own passion. His hearers knew the Roman cross as an instrument of shame; he turns it into the sign of the disciple. Then comes the paradox at the heart of the faith: “Those who find their life will lose it, and those who lose their life for my sake will find it.” The midwives of Egypt lost their safety and found the lives of children. And then the tone changes, and the discourse ends with welcome. “Whoever welcomes you welcomes me, and whoever welcomes me welcomes the one who sent me.” It is a chain of presence: the Father, the Son, the disciple, the host. A prophet or a righteous person welcomed in his name brings a reward, “and whoever gives even a cup of cold water to one of these little ones in the name of a disciple ... none of these will lose their reward.” The smallest hospitality counts: in Kerala, the people who set up water-sheds for travellers in the hot months know what a cup of cold water is worth. “Now when Jesus had finished instructing his twelve disciples, he went on from there to teach and proclaim his message in their cities.” The instruction is done; the teacher goes on preaching. When, many years later, Herod will try to kill another child, the Holy Family will go down into Egypt for refuge (Matthew 2:13–15), and the land of Pharaoh will again shelter a Hebrew child.
outline: Ask: who are the people in your country or neighbourhood whom someone has decided are a threat, and what does the Bible say about them?
Point 1 · A king who did not know Joseph
Forgetting the good done by others leads to fear, and fear to oppression.
Point 2 · The more they were oppressed
God's blessing grows under the whip; the midwives refuse to kill.
Point 3 · Not peace but a sword
Jesus cuts through every loyalty that stands above him.
Point 4 · A cup of cold water
The smallest welcome given in his name is never lost.
live: Write the names of three people to whom you owe your life, your faith or your livelihood, and thank at least one of them this week, in person or by a call.
Offer a cup of cold water (Matthew 10:42)
Do one small act of hospitality for a stranger or a worker: a glass of water, a seat, a meal, a kind word, in the name of Christ.
2027-07-12.prayer: Lord God of the oppressed, you saw the misery of your people in Egypt and you did not let the whip or the river destroy them. Give us a good memory, so that we may never forget those who have served us. Give us fearless consciences, like the midwives who feared you more than the king. Lord Jesus, you did not come to bring a false peace; teach us to love you above every other love, and to take up the cross and follow you. Bless those who give a cup of cold water in your name, and those who receive it. Our help is in your name, Lord, who made heaven and earth. Amen.
altar: The Church has long prayed these very words from the Psalm: “Our help is in the name of the Lord,” and the people answer, “Who made heaven and earth.” In the older form of the Mass the priest says them at the foot of the altar. At the Eucharist we remember what the Lord has done, as the Israelites remembered their bitter slavery each Passover, and we hear his words, “Do this in memory of me.” He is the one who does not forget us. And the Eucharist is the cup of cold water, and much more, that he gives us: “Whoever welcomes me welcomes the one who sent me.”

quick: A new king who does not know Joseph fears the Israelites, makes them slaves and orders that every Hebrew boy be thrown into the Nile; but the more they are oppressed, the more they multiply.
Psalm 124 gives thanks that the Lord was on Israel's side and that the snare is broken: our help is in the name of the Lord.
Jesus says he brings not peace but a sword that divides, asks to be loved above everything, and promises a reward even for a cup of cold water given in his name.
2027-07-12.action: Give a cup of cold water, in some form, to someone who needs it today.
2027-07-12.question: Is there anyone I have stopped thanking, or anyone I have begun to fear, because of what I have forgotten?

family.explain: A long time after Joseph had died, a new king ruled Egypt who did not remember the good Joseph had done. He was afraid of the Israelites, and he made them work very hard as slaves. But God was with them, and they became even stronger. Two brave women, Shiphrah and Puah, would not obey the king when he told them to hurt the babies. They obeyed God. Jesus says that every kind thing we do for others, even giving a cup of cold water, is seen by God and will never be lost.
family.intention: We pray for children and workers who are made to work too hard, and for everyone who is afraid of strangers.
family.ask: Ask: “Who has helped our family in the past, so that we may thank them? And who needs a cup of water from us today?”

illus: At a brick kiln near a town in Kerala, a priest on a Sunday visit met a group of migrant workers who had come from another state to work there during the dry months. They lived in huts by the kiln and had been told that the weekly day of rest was a luxury. The priest asked for nothing except to sit with them; a woman from the parish had sent a large flask of tea and some banana chips. A young man who had not been home for nine months said afterwards that he could not remember the last time someone had asked his name. The woman from the parish was invited to the kiln the next week, and she went, not alone, but with her children. (An illustrative story.)

pm.open: Lord God, you saw the misery of your people and came down to deliver them. Lord Jesus, you tell us to welcome one another in your name. Be with us. Amen.
share: A new king arose over Egypt, who did not know Joseph (Exodus 1:8). What good done to me by others have I forgotten, and who might need my gratitude?
The more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied (Exodus 1:12). Where have I seen God's life grow in the face of hardship?
The midwives feared God (Exodus 1:17). When have I been asked to do something wrong, and what helped me to refuse?
Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me (Matthew 10:37). What is the one thing I find hardest to put second to Christ?
Whoever gives even a cup of cold water to one of these little ones (Matthew 10:42). Who is a little one who needs a welcome from me?
pm.resp: Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth.
interc: For the Church, that she may never forget the poor, and may be a home for refugees, migrants and workers who are not welcome elsewhere.
For all who suffer forced labour, trafficking and slavery in our own time, and for those who work to bring them release.
For those who refuse to carry out unjust orders at a cost to themselves, and for midwives, doctors and nurses who protect life.
For families divided by faith, that they may find peace and respect without betraying Christ.
For our group, that we may be quick to give a cup of cold water in his name.
pm.close: Father, you hear the cry of the oppressed and you are our help. Teach us to welcome others as we welcome you. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, a new chapter begins today. A new king arose over Egypt, who did not know Joseph (Exodus 1:8). Joseph had saved the country in the famine. But a new generation has forgotten him. How quickly we forget those who did us good. And the king is afraid. Look, he says, the Israelites are too many. They may join our enemies. So he deals shrewdly with them: forced labour, hard work in mortar and brick, and at last the order to throw the baby boys into the Nile. When we forget, we begin to fear; when we fear, we begin to oppress.

But the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied (Exodus 1:12). You cannot stop the blessing of God with a decree. And God has allies in unexpected places: two midwives, Shiphrah and Puah, who feared God and let the boys live. The Bible gives their names, and forgets the king's. Whenever you see the powerful oppressing the weak, remember the midwives. Small people who say no can change the course of history.

In the Gospel Jesus speaks plainly: I have not come to bring peace, but a sword (Matthew 10:34). He means: following me will cut through everything, even the dearest loyalties. Nobody and nothing may stand above God. And whoever does not take up the cross and follow me is not worthy of me. Those who find their life will lose it, and those who lose their life for my sake will find it (Matthew 10:39). The midwives lost their safety and found the lives of many children.

But the passage ends with welcome. Whoever welcomes you welcomes me, and whoever welcomes me welcomes the one who sent me. And a cup of cold water. Such a small thing. Yet Jesus says: none of these will lose their reward. This week, let us do a small thing for someone nobody welcomes, a migrant, a worker, a stranger. And let us give thanks to those who have done us good, and whom we may have forgotten. Amen.
kids: Children, a long time after Joseph, there was a new king in Egypt, and he forgot everything good that Joseph had done. He was afraid of the Israelites, and he made them work as slaves. But two brave women, Shiphrah and Puah, would not do what the king said, because they loved God. God was pleased with them. Jesus tells his friends: whoever gives even a cup of cold water to someone in my name will get a reward from God. A smile, a glass of water, a hello to someone who is new: Jesus sees all of these!

intro: A king who forgets, midwives who refuse, a sword that cuts through every loyalty, and a cup of cold water that is never lost.

points.h: A king who did not know Joseph
sub: Forced labour and a river of death.
q: Now a new king arose over Egypt, who did not know Joseph.
Then he took a loaf of bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and gave it to them, saying, “This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.”
points.apply: Thank, this week, one person who did you good long ago.

sub: The Church grows under the cross.
q: But the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied and spread, so that the Egyptians came to dread the Israelites.
We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed;
points.apply: Say no this week to one small injustice that you are asked to go along with.

q: for the son treats the father with contempt, the daughter rises up against her mother, the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; your enemies are members of your own household.
Do not think that I have come to bring peace to the earth; I have not come to bring peace, but a sword.
points.apply: Name the one loyalty or habit that stands in the way of following Christ, and ask for the courage to put it second.

q: We have escaped like a bird from the snare of the fowlers; the snare is broken, and we have escaped.
Whoever welcomes you welcomes me, and whoever welcomes me welcomes the one who sent me.
points.apply: Give a cup of cold water in some form to a worker or a stranger this week.

concl: A king forgets Joseph and oppresses the Hebrews, but God's blessing grows, and two midwives refuse to obey; Psalm 124 sings: our help is in the name of the Lord.
Jesus asks to be loved above all, promises that we shall find our life by losing it, and says that a cup of cold water given in his name will not lose its reward.
2027-07-12.resolve: Thank one person you have forgotten, and give one act of welcome to a stranger.
